TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) and UDP (User Datagram Protocol) are the two most common transport-layer protocols in the IP suite. They define how data is packaged, addressed, transmitted, and received between applications over a network. The fundamental difference is that TCP provides a reliable, ordered, and error-checked stream of data, while UDP offers a lightweight, connectionless datagram service with no guarantees.

### Comparison Table: TCP vs UDP

| Feature                  | TCP (Transmission Control Protocol)                           | UDP (User Datagram Protocol)                               |
|--------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Connection type**      | Connection-oriented – a connection is established before data transfer (three-way handshake). | Connectionless – data is sent without establishing a connection. |
| **Reliability**          | Reliable – guarantees delivery of data. Lost packets are retransmitted. | Unreliable – no guarantee of delivery, no retransmission. |
| **Ordering**             | Maintains strict order of data segments. Data arrives in the same sequence it was sent. | No ordering guarantees. Packets may arrive out of order. |
| **Error checking**       | Extensive error checking using checksums, acknowledgements (ACKs), and timeouts. Corrupt segments are retransmitted. | Basic error checking via a checksum (optional in IPv4, mandatory in IPv6). Corrupt packets are silently discarded. |
| **Flow control**         | Yes – uses a sliding window mechanism to prevent overwhelming the receiver. | No flow control. Sender can transmit data at any rate. |
| **Congestion control**   | Yes – algorithms (slow start, congestion avoidance, fast retransmit) adjust transmission rate to avoid network congestion. | No congestion control. Can flood the network if not managed by the application. |
| **Speed / Overhead**     | Slower due to connection setup, acknowledgements, and retransmissions. Higher overhead (20-byte header minimum). | Faster, lower latency. Minimal overhead (8-byte header). |
| **Data boundary**        | Stream-oriented – data is a continuous stream of bytes without message boundaries. | Message-oriented – each datagram is an independent message with preserved boundaries. |
| **Header size**          | 20–60 bytes (20 bytes without options).                      | 8 bytes fixed.                                             |
| **Handshake**            | Three-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK) to establish connection; four-way termination. | No handshake.                                              |
| **Broadcast / Multicast**| Not supported – TCP is strictly unicast (point-to-point).    | Supports broadcast and multicast.                          |
| **Typical use cases**    | Web browsing (HTTP/HTTPS), email (SMTP, IMAP), file transfers (FTP), remote administration (SSH), databases. | Streaming media (VoIP, video), online gaming, DNS queries, DHCP, real-time communications, IoT sensor data. |
| **State management**     | Maintains connection state (sequence numbers, buffers, timers) on both ends. | Stateless – no connection state maintained by the protocol. |

In short, choose **TCP** when you need guaranteed, ordered delivery and can tolerate some latency (e.g., loading a web page, sending an email). Choose **UDP** when speed and low latency are critical and occasional data loss is acceptable (e.g., live video calls, online games, DNS lookups).
